notes.meaning: God warned Aaron that he, his sons, and his family line would answer for any harm or defilement that came to the sanctuary. They alone would also carry the blame if they failed in their duties as priests. This heavy responsibility showed that Aaron's high office was a serious burden rather than something for other people to envy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the priests faced the greatest danger because their daily work near the holiest things put them constantly at risk of ritual mistakes.

notes.meaning: God told Aaron to bring the rest of the tribe of Levi to help with the work of the sacred tent. The name Levi carries the idea of being joined together, and they were joined to Aaron to assist him. While the Levites helped with daily tasks, Aaron and his sons retained the unique duty of serving as priests.

The Levites were assigned to assist Aaron and care for the Tent, but they were strictly forbidden from going near the altar or the holy furnishings. If a Levite touched those sacred items, both that Levite and the priests who permitted it would die. God protected the sacredness of his worship by establishing firm boundaries between these offices.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary emphasizes that the Levites were barred from offering the actual sacrifice and sprinkling blood, which belonged to the priests alone.

notes.meaning: The Levites were to work alongside the priests in taking care of the Tent of Meeting. At the same time, any outsider who did not belong to the tribe of Levi was kept far away from these duties. This protective guard kept the rest of the community from wandering into holy spaces and facing sudden judgment.

Aaron and his sons were commanded to guard the sanctuary and the altar with great care. By carrying out their duties faithfully, they would keep God's anger from falling on the people of Israel again. Faithful ministry shields God's people from spiritual danger.

God reminded Aaron that the Levites had been chosen from the whole nation as a special gift to him. They were dedicated directly to the Lord so they could handle the heavy physical labor required at the Tent of Meeting. Good helpers in the work of God are a gracious blessing from above.

Aaron and his sons alone were granted the privilege to minister at the altar and enter behind the inner curtain. God described their priesthood as a gift of pure grace, not an honor they had earned for themselves. Any outsider who dared to step in and take over that sacred work had to be put to death.

God placed Aaron in charge of the sacred contributions brought by the people of Israel, giving them to him and his sons as their regular portion. They received these gifts because they were anointed and set apart for the Lord's service. Those who give their lives to God's work can trust him to provide for their daily needs.

The priests were given the portions of the most holy offerings that were not burned up on the altar. This included leftover parts of grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings brought to make things right with God. These sacred food portions belonged entirely to Aaron and his sons as his appointed servants.

The priests were instructed to eat these most holy offerings only in the sacred court of the Tabernacle. Only the male members of the priestly families were permitted to eat them, because these gifts required the highest reverence. God taught his servants to treat sacred gifts with deep respect.

God also assigned to Aaron the special wave offerings presented by the people. Unlike the most holy gifts, these foods could be eaten at home by both sons and daughters, provided they were ceremonially clean. Being clean meant they were free from any ritual defilement that made a person unfit to touch holy food.

The priests were given the very best and freshest olive oil, new wine, and grain brought as firstfruits. The firstfruits were the earliest and finest harvest gathered from the land and offered to the Lord. Providing these gifts to God's ministers showed that God always deserves the best part of our labor.

All the earliest ripe produce that the Israelites brought to the Lord belonged to Aaron's household. Any family member who was ceremonially clean was allowed to eat from these fresh harvests. God generously fed the families of those who dedicated their lives to his worship.

Everything in Israel that was permanently devoted to the Lord by a vow became the property of the priests. This included usable goods and consumable produce, while dedicated metal treasures were reserved for the Tabernacle itself. Gifts devoted to God went directly to support his holy work.

The firstborn male of every womb, whether human or animal, belonged to the Lord and was brought to the priest. However, human children and unclean animals could never be offered on the altar, so God commanded that they be redeemed. To redeem meant paying a set price to buy the life back for the family.

The redemption price for a one-month-old baby boy was fixed at five silver shekels. This standard price ensured that every family paid the exact same amount before the Lord, whether rich or poor. It served as a regular reminder that every human life belongs to God.

The firstborn of clean farm animals—cattle, sheep, and goats—could not be bought back with money. Because they were holy to God, their blood had to be sprinkled against the altar and their fat burned as a sweet-smelling fire offering. These animals were dedicated directly to God in sacred sacrifice.

After the fat of these clean animals was burned on the altar, all the meat was given to the priests. This was given to them in the same way as the breast and right leg of the peace offerings. God made sure his ministers were well supplied from the sacrifices brought by the people.

God established this support for the priestly families as a permanent rule, describing it as a covenant of salt. In the ancient world, salt stood for permanence and incorruption because it preserved meat from spoiling. God's promise to provide for his servants and their children is secure and cannot be broken.

The Lord told Aaron that the priests would receive no tract of land as an inheritance when Israel entered Canaan. Instead, the Lord himself was their portion and their special inheritance among the tribes. Those who have the Lord as their greatest treasure need not depend on earthly land.

God granted all the tithes in Israel to the Levites as their tribal inheritance. A tithe was a tenth of the grain, fruit, and animals given by the people each year. This was their rightful wage for doing the demanding work of the Tent of Meeting on behalf of the whole nation.

differ.view: Many Baptists teach that the Old Testament tithe was tied to the Levitical priesthood and that Christians today are called to voluntary, generous giving rather than a mandatory ten percent.
Many Presbyterians and Reformed teachers hold that the ten percent tithe began before Moses and remains God's ongoing standard and baseline for Christian stewardship today.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Thomas Aquinas argued that the Christian clergy are the spiritual successors of the Levites, so tithes were owed to support them, though modern canon law requires general financial support rather than a strict ten percent.

notes.meaning: Ordinary Israelites were forbidden to approach the Tent of Meeting to carry out sacred services. If they attempted to take over those duties, they would bring guilt upon themselves and die. Keeping a respectful distance preserved both the holiness of God's house and the lives of the people.

The Levites alone were to do the work of the Tent of Meeting, and they would bear the penalty if they were careless in guarding it. Because their full-time job was to protect and serve the sanctuary, they received no territory of land among the other tribes. They were called to live by trusting God's steady provision through the community.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church fathers such as Cyprian saw the Levites' freedom from land as a model for Christian clergy, who should stay unentangled by worldly business in order to focus on ministry.

notes.meaning: God explained that the tithes presented by the Israelites were given directly to the Levites as their inheritance. They received this income from God himself, not as a favor or handout from the other tribes. Serving the Lord was treated as honest labor that earned a secure living.

The Lord gave these next instructions directly to Moses rather than Aaron. Because Aaron and his sons would receive the tithes from the Levites, having Moses deliver the command ensured everything was fair and above suspicion. God manages the support of his ministers with complete transparency.

Moses instructed the Levites that when they received the tithes from the Israelites, they had to give a tenth of that tithe as an offering to the Lord. Even though they lived on the gifts of others, they were not excused from worshiping God with their own possessions. Everyone who receives God's blessings is called to be a giver.

God promised that this tithe of the tithe from the Levites would be counted just like fresh grain from a threshing floor or juice from a winepress. Even though they had not plowed the fields or pressed the grapes, God fully accepted their contribution. The Lord values a willing heart, no matter how our income is earned.

The Levites were to hand over the Lord's tenth of the tithes directly to Aaron the priest. This ensured that the priests serving at the altar were supported by the Levites, just as the Levites were supported by the people. God organized his house so that all his workers were cared for in turn.

The Levites were required to choose the very best and choicest parts of all the tithes they received to offer to the Lord. They were never to keep the finest produce for themselves and pass along the second-rate goods to the priests. God always deserves our highest quality and our deepest devotion.

Moses told the Levites that after they gave the best part to the priests, the rest of the tithe was theirs to use freely. It would be credited to them just like the normal crop of any farmer in Israel. Giving to God first brings freedom and peace to our daily living.

The Levites and their families were allowed to eat the remaining food anywhere they wished, since it was not restricted to the sanctuary court. It was their proper wage for the hard work they performed at the Tent of Meeting. God provides an honest reward for those who labor in his house.

As long as the Levites offered the best part to God and the priests, they were free from guilt when eating the rest of the food. However, if they were selfish and held back God's holy portion, they would defile the sacred gifts and die. Honoring God with our resources brings life rather than judgment.
